name: Macau
why: OpenRice covers Macau as well as Hong Kong.

spots.name: Ruins of St. Paul's Cathedral
spots.desc: The city's most famous landmark and is regarded as the greatest monument to Christianity in the East. The only thing left of the Church of Mater Dei, built in the 1600s but burnt down in 1835, is the imposing façade, with its Biblical statues and relief, being described as a "sermon in stone" and a "Bible for the poor". Nearby are the remains of the St Paul's College. Behind the façade is the…

spots.name: Grand Lisboa
spots.desc: A prominent, 261m tall hotel located right next to the famed Casino Lisboa, effectively an extension of it. It's the tallest building in Macau and with the lotus shape also most distinctive part of its skyline. Inside, a 218 carat diamond The Star of Stanley Ho is on permanent display.

spots.name: Macau Tower
spots.local: 澳門旅遊塔會展娛樂中心
spots.desc: You'll get a great view over Macau and Taipa. There is a viewing platform outside and an inside platform with glass floor panels, and a cafe. AJ Hackett also runs "adventure" activities on the tower (see "Do" below).

spots.name: A-Ma Temple
spots.desc: Perhaps the most famous Chinese temple in Macau. This is a Taoist temple which predates the Portuguese era. The name "Macau" is believed to be a Portuguese mispronunciation of the temple's Cantonese name.

spots.name: The Venetian Macao Resort Hotel
spots.local: 澳門威尼斯人度假村酒店
spots.desc: The Venetian is touted as the largest casino, and fourth largest building, in the world by floor area. At a cost of nearly $2.4bn, it is hardly a surprise. There are close to 3,000 suites, 16,000 staff members, 840 gaming tables and 3,400 slot machines. In addition it has a 15,000-seat sports arena. The concept is Venice meets China and there are even indoor canals replete with gondola and sampan…

spots.name: St. Dominic's Church
spots.desc: The pastel-coloured church was founded in 1587 by Spanish Dominican priests. The bell tower at the back of the building has been converted into the small Museum of Sacred Art with around 300 artifacts.

spots.name: Mount Fortress
spots.desc: Built between 1617 and 1626 by the Jesuits, the fortress one of the main defence structures of the city. It housed barracks, arsenal and storehouses to allow it to withstand a siege lasting two years. You can get good views of the central part of Macau Peninsula from here. The fortress can be accessed by escalator just east of St Paul's. The Macau Museum is located within the fortress (see…

spots.name: Wynn Macau
spots.desc: On 6 September 2006 Wynn's huge casino/hotel/resort complex opened, and many expect it to soon surpass all of its rivals in gambling income. Every 15 minutes there are short fountain shows in front of the hotel with music, spraying fountains and the occasional bursts of flame—go after dark for the spectacular lights that are part of the show. The casino is beautiful with mostly slot machines and…

spots.name: Sé Cathedral
spots.desc: No records of the exact date of construction exist but a solid brick structure was built on this site in 1622 and repaied in 1743. The cathedral has some impressive stained glass murals and the facade is characterised by its twin belfries. The exterior is clad in Shanghai plaster which gives the church a subdued appearance.

spots.name: Senate Square
spots.desc: A colorful typical Iberian town square, this is the traditional heart of Macau city, complete with the traditional Portuguese pavement. It is surrounded by pastel-coloured neo-classical buildings, most of them having an administrative function during the Portuguese era. The place is a popular venue for public events and crowds gather here just to soak in the atmosphere and socialise.

spots.name: Loyal Senate
spots.desc: Built to house Macau's municipal government, the Leal Senado has a neo-classical design and much of the original layout and structure has been retained through the years. The first floor has a ceremonial meeting room that adjoins an elaborate library. The name "Loyal Senate" is derived from the name bestowed upon Macau - "City of Our Name of God Macau, There is None More Loyal" - by King Dom João…

spots.name: Guia Fortress
spots.desc: Built in the 1600s on top of Guia Hill on the eastern part of the peninsula, the fortress's main function was to ward off any attack by China. Within the fortress is the Chapel of Our Lady of Guia and the 15 m-tall Guia Lighthouse, said to be the first modern lighthouse on the Chinese coast. Guia Fortress can be reached by the Guia Cable Car (Teleférico da Guia) just outside the entrance of the…

spots.name: Sands Macau
spots.desc: The Sands offers a more open Las Vegas feel along with a smoke-free gaming room, the Pearl Room. Tables at the Sands play almost exclusively in HKD.

spots.name: Dom Pedro V Theatre
spots.desc: Built in 1860 as the first Western-style theatre on the Chinese coast, it remains a significant cultural landmark of the Macanese community and remains a venue for many public functions and events.

spots.name: Old Protestant Cemetery
spots.desc: Lovely little piece of England in Macau. Look out for the grave of the Right Honourable Lord H.I. Spencer Churchill, ancestor of Winston Churchill, and also for the graves of the painter George Chinnery (far left in the upper row) and the missionary Robert Morrison (far right near the back; his accomplishments include writing the first Chinese-English, English-Chinese dictionary).

spots.name: Macau Mosque and Cemetery
spots.desc: The only mosque in Macau. The complex also houses the city's only Muslim cemetery and the office of Islamic Association of Macau.
spots.addr: No. 4, Ramal Dos Moros, Nossa Senhora de Fátima

spots.name: Macau Museum
spots.price: MOP15; free for children 12 and under and seniors 65 and older

spots.name: City of Dreams
spots.desc: a large clump of hotels, casinos, restaurants and entertainment venues located just across a road from the Venetian. As elsewhere in the strip, there is quite a wide choice of restaurants, mostly upmarket, with many different styles of food.

spots.name: Na Tcha Temple
spots.desc: Tucked in the corner of a cobblestone square to the left of (as you face) the ruins of St. Paul's is this tiny temple dedicated to the Chinese deity Prince Nata. The juxtaposition of Catholic church and traditional Chinese temple is a perfect example of Macau's contrasts and multicultural history.

spots.name: Casino Lisboa
spots.desc: The grand old dame of Macau's casinos, the Lisboa offers an older world feel on its gaming floors, structured in a labyrinth of different clubs and rooms for various levels of play, with displays of antiques owned by the late gambling tycoon Stanley Ho. Tables play in both MOP and HKD.

spots.name: St. Joseph's Seminary and Church
spots.desc: Established in 1728, the old Seminary, together with St Paul's College, was the base of missionary work in China, Japan and other parts of the region. The adjacent church was built in 1758 and is noted for its Baroque architecture.

spots.name: Holy House of Mercy
spots.desc: This building, established by the firsty Bishop of Macau in 1569, provides an imposing façade for the Senate Square. The building houses a charitable organisation which looked after the medical, social and welfare needs of the citizens of Macau, and was the home of many orphans and prostitutes. Today, it houses a two-room museum with displays of items related to the organisation.

spots.name: Wynn Palace
spots.desc: Like its counterpart on the Macau Peninsula, the Wynn Palace has a performance lake with light and fountain shows. The fountains do some low-key dancing constantly, but the real shows, set to music, are every 20–30 minutes and are more spectacular than the ones at the other Wynn. The hotel/casino also has cable cars that carry you through the air around the performance lake on your way into the…

spots.name: Macau Dome
spots.desc: Is a bowling centre of international standard, constructed in 2005 for the East Asian Games. There are 24 lanes, the first four of which may be used by children as these lanes are equipped with raisable borders. A lane costs MOP20 per person a game during the day, MOP30 in the evening. The Macau Dome can be reached from Macau and Taipa by bus 21, 21A, 25, 26, or 26A, or from Taipa by bus 15 (get…

spots.name: Sir Robert Ho Tung Library
spots.desc: Built as the residence of a Portuguese Dona, it was purchased by Hong Kong businessman Sir Robert Ho Tung as a retreat. When he passed away, he willed the building to be passed over to the Macau government to be turned into a public library.

spots.name: Portas do Cerco
spots.desc: Called the Barrier Gate in Chinese, the Portuguese name "Gate of Siege" says a lot more to the hundreds of years of relations between the Portuguese and Chinese. The old archway, built in 1870, marked the border between Portuguese and Chinese territory, and was the actual border crossing between Macau and China until 1994, when a new crossing by the side was created. The archway and surroundings…

spots.name: St. Anthony's Church
spots.desc: One of Macau's oldest churches, the first structure was built of wood and bamboo. The current structure was constructed in 1930.

spots.name: Casa Garden
spots.desc: This house, built in 1770, was the residence of the wealthy Portuguese merchant Manuel Pereira and was later rented out to the English East India Company. Today, it is the headquarters of the Oriental Foundation.

spots.name: Chapel of Our Lady of Penha and Penha Hill
spots.desc: The chapel sits atop a steep hill which towers above the southernmost tip of Macau Peninsula. From the various lookouts from the hill, you'll get excellent views of the central area of Macau, Nam Van and Sai Van lakes, Macau Tower, the three Macau-Taipa bridges and across the Pearl River into China.

spots.name: Moorish Barracks
spots.desc: Built in 1874 to accommodate an Indian regiment from Goa, it now serves as the headquarters of the Macau Maritime Authority.

spots.name: St. Augustine's Church
spots.desc: Established by the Spanish Augustinians in 1591, this church maintains the tradition of organising the Easter Procession around the city.

spots.name: Lou Kau Mansion
spots.desc: Built in 1889, this was the home of Lou Kau, a prominent Chinese merchant who owned several properties in the city. The architecture is that of a typical Chinese residential building.

spots.name: Lou Lim Ioc
spots.desc: Beautiful garden sanctuary on the peninsula of Macau. It was part of an old Chinese mansion reconverted to museum and art gallery.

spots.name: Golden Lotus Square
spots.desc: Public square with a large golden sculpture of a lotus in full bloom to commemorate the handover of Macau from Portugal back to China on 20th December 1999. There is a flag raising ceremony held here at 8AM every morning by the Macau Police. Despite that fact that Macau is now under Chinese sovereignty, the Macau Police continue to perform Portuguese instead of Chinese foot drills.

spots.name: Seac Pai Van Park
spots.desc: This 20 hectare park along Estrada Seac Pai Van just south of the Taipa-Coloane Isthmus Causeway, has a medicinal garden as well as other green areas, a mini zoo and a lake. The Museum of Nature and Agriculture is located within the park, as is the Macao Giant Panda Pavilion (MOP10, free for seniors 65 and older and for children 12 and under).

spots.name: Hac Sa
spots.desc: Hac Sa beach, the larger of the two, in a bay with the Grand Coloane resort on its eastern end. The water is of mediocre quality but brave swimmers can enter the water here. Those less brave choose the swimming pool just opposite the beach.

spots.name: Section of the Old City Walls
spots.desc: This is a segment of the city's defence structures built in 1569, which has survived. It is built with a compound material called chunambo, a mixture of clay, soil, sand, rice straw, crushed rocks and oyster shells which were placed in layers.

spots.name: Macau Government Headquarters
spots.desc: Built in 1849 as a nobleman's residence, it was the official palace of the Governor of Macau. The building now hosts the Chief Executive's Office. There are usually opening days that lasts for 2 days in each year October when travellers can enter the building.

spots.name: Museum of Taipa and Coloane History
spots.desc: Contains detailed and informative displays of the two islands.
spots.price: Entry is M$5 and is open 10am to 6pm every day except Monday

spots.name: Sun Yat Sen Memorial House
spots.desc: Dr. Sun Yat Sen's residence when he was practicing medicine in Macau, and later the place where his family lived. While called a museum, the Moorish-style building hosts very little exhibition apart from furniture at that time and personal correspondence.

spots.name: Red Market
spots.local: 紅街市, Mercado Municipal Almirante Lacerda
spots.desc: The Red Market is a bustling market in a big red brick building, where vendors sell food of every conceivable kind. The ground floor is mostly produce, the first floor is fish, and the second floor is meat.

spots.name: Maritime Museum
spots.desc: With exhibits on Macau's seafaring history.

spots.name: Fire Services Museum
spots.desc: Built as the headquarters of the Fire Services Bureau, the historical building is now a museum dedicated to the history of the fire brigade and hosts a variety of antique fire engines and firefighting apparatus. Closed from public admittance as of October 2024. The rebuilt Central Fire Station is in use and next to the museum.

spots.name: St. Augustine's Square
spots.desc: This square is fronted by various pretty buildings of Macau's past era, namely the St Augustine's Church, Dom Pedro V Theatre, St Joseph's Seminary and Church and the Robert Ho Tung Library.

spots.name: The House of Dancing Water
spots.desc: A 90-minute water-based performance of a love story with acrobatics and elaborate special effects.

spots.name: Taipa Houses Museum
spots.local: 龍環葡韻住宅式博物館
spots.desc: Made up of a row of colonial houses from the early 20th century. They have been restored and preserved inside showing the style of living of the original owners.

spots.name: Quartel de São Francisco/Museum of the Macao Security Forces
spots.local: 加思欄兵營/澳門保安部隊博物館
spots.desc: A museum showing the history of Macau's first responders, which was built as a Portuguese barracks and later the headquarters of the security forces. Exhibition includes firearms, uniforms and various policing and firefighting equipment. Entry requires ID registration and X-ray scanning.

spots.name: Dumbo Restaurant
spots.desc: Dumbo Restaurant serves Macau style Portuguese food that is famous in Macau. From curry crab, fried eel, steak grilled with onion, pork cutlet cooked in tomato sauce.

spots.name: Irish Bar
spots.desc: This is the place to head for a true Irish tavern experience – the bar is dark, service friendly, booths cozy, and it has one of Macau’s best ranges of draught beer.
spots.addr: Av. De Kwong Tung no. 116C-D G/F

spots.name: Pou Tai Un
spots.desc: A Buddhist temple with a vegetarian Buddhist restaurant.

spots.name: Four-Faced Buddha
spots.desc: A shrine from Thailand.

spots.name: The Londoner Macao
spots.desc: Resort complex including five hotels (The Londoner Hotel, Londoner Court, Conrad Hilton, St. Regis and Sheraton Grand) and replicas of Elizabeth Tower (better known as Big Ben), the Houses of Parliament and Crystal Palace.

spots.name: Coloane Village
spots.desc: Quiet and lazy, Coloane Village, the main village on the island, is a joy to just walk around and explore. Its narrow lanes lined with pastel-coloured houses and shops. Avenida de Cinco de Outubro is the main esplanade where you can look across the narrow channel to Hengqin Island in China. Along this street you will find the pretty Chapel of St Francis set back from the road by a square flanked…

spots.name: A-Ma Statue
spots.desc: The 20m statue is situated near the 172.4m Alto de Coloane and was erected in 1998. Adjacent to it is a large, quiet temple. The statue and temple can be reached via Estrada do Alto de Coloane or by walking the Coloane trail.

spots.name: Cheoc Van
spots.desc: This is the smaller and more beautiful beach. The sand here is golden and more inviting to sunbathe or play on. There is a nice curved swimming pool just by the beach (as opposed to the traditional rectangular one at Hac Sa). A cordoned-off area of the bay is set aside for swimmers, and members of the Winter Swimmers Association go swimming here daily (yes, even in the coldest of winter!).

spots.name: Fernando's
spots.desc: Traditional Portuguese food, especially barbecue and seafood: lots of salty bacalhau (dried cod) and clams. Neither the decor nor the food are fancy, and it's expensive for what you get, but it's a Macau institution and has a devoted following. Just off Hac Sa beach, with a courtyard bar at the back.

spots.name: Lord Stow's Bakery
spots.desc: Sit-down cafe and a bakery at the Village Square. A Macau institution, Lord Stow's is famous for its cheesecakes, fruitcakes, sandwiches, and most of all, its Macanese egg tarts, which are now available from franchises throughout Asia.

spots.name: Nga Tim
spots.desc: What a beautiful outdoor setting! Located in the colonnade on the left as you face St. Francis Xavier Church, the restaurant serves up authentic Portuguese and Chinese fare with views of the church plaza and the waterfront. Popular with tourists and locals, they accept credit cards and are reasonably priced.
spots.addr: Edificio Fong U, 8 R. do Caetano

spots.name: Pousada de Coloane
spots.desc: Pousada de Coloane, and facing the picturesque Cheoc Van Beach, this splendid restaurant serves delicious, home-style Portuguese cuisine in a lovely environment.
spots.addr: Pousada de Coloane, Praia de Cheoc Van, Colane Island

spots.name: Food Paradise
spots.desc: A food court with a good range of choices generally at better prices than elsewhere in Cotai, albeit with less sumptuous decor and service.

spots.name: Blue Frog Bar and Grill
spots.desc: Outlet of the famous Shanghai joint, with large portions of American food plus one of the widest selections of shots, cocktails, liquor and wines in Macau.

spots.name: Lilau Square
spots.desc: Pretty little square surrounded by the old Mediterranean-style houses of one of Macau's oldest residential areas. The square has a spring where it is said that "One who drinks from Lilau never forgets Macau".

spots.name: Mandarin House
spots.desc: The Macau Mandarin House is the former residence owned by eminent modern Chinese thinker Zheng Guanying and his father Zheng Wenrui. The house was built in around 1881 and over time, many families occupied the complex. It covers an area of about 4,000 sq metres and is a traditional Chinese-style compound containing a number of buildings

spots.name: St. Lawrence's Church
spots.desc: Built in the mid 16th century, this is one of the oldest churches in Macau. Families of Portuguese sailors used to gather on its front steps and pray and wait for the safe return of their loved ones.

spots.name: Sam Kai Vui Kun Temple
spots.desc: Located close to the Chinese Bazaar area, this temple has some Western styles to its architecture, illustrating the harmonious coexistence of the two cultures in this city. The temple has a long association with Chinese business associations and guilds.
spots.addr: Rua Sul do Mercado de Sao Domingos

spots.name: Cemetério de São Miguel Arcanjo
spots.desc: A classic example of Sino-Portuguese Culture. A great place for lovers of angel statues.

spots.name: Kun Iam Temple
spots.desc: A large, old Buddhist temple to the north of downtown. It's a little out of the way, but is definitely worth a visit if you're into temples.

spots.name: Kun Iam Statue
spots.desc: Twenty metre high bronze statue of the Goddess of Mercy emerging from a lotus floating in the Outer Harbour. The statue is connected to land by a 60 m footbridge.

spots.name: Wine Museum and Grand Prix Museum
spots.desc: The Wine Museum and the Grand Prix Museum are both in the same building, north of the center of town.

spots.name: Luís de Camões Garden and Grotto
spots.desc: One of the largest gardens in Macau, the land used to be owned by the British East India Company and was bought over by a Portuguese merchant who then willed it to the Macau government to be turned into a public garden when he died. The garden was dedicated to master Lusitan poet Luís de Camões. The gardens are popular with tai chi and aerobics groups and also people who bring their birds in…

spots.name: Rua da Felicidade
spots.desc: The old red light district. Today it is a fairly interesting shopping street, with various antiques and handicrafts, and is also popular with movie makers: the Shanghai Nightclub car chase scene from Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom was filmed here, including parts of the main street, Avenida de Almeida Ribeiro.

spots.name: Avenida da República
spots.desc: One of the most beautiful avenues in Macau, this tree-lined road arcs around the southernmost tip of the peninsula and is the address of some of the most pretty Portuguese residential buildings in the territory, all of them enjoying an unobstructed view of the Nam Van and Sai Van lakes. The world-acclaimed Pousada de São Tiago, with its access staircase through the walls of the ruined Barra…

spots.name: Three Lamps
spots.desc: Three Lamps and surrounding narrow streets are full of tiny shops selling many kinds of goods at bargain prices.

spots.name: Wong Chi Kei
spots.desc: A good place to go to fill up with rice and noodles. Open till late.

spots.name: Noodle and Congee Corner
spots.desc: It's more like a restaurant than a "corner" and they prepare various style noodles while you (can) watch. Excellent quality and quite reasonable for such a special treat.

spots.name: Sing Hoi
spots.desc: Serves mostly Chinese food but has a handful of Portuguese dishes on offer. The Portuguese baked chicken (MOP40) is delicious.
spots.addr: Avenida Xian Xing Hai, 冼星海大马路

spots.name: Su You Pin Wei
spots.desc: A tiny, very casual vegetarian restaurant. The atmosphere is of a low-key social event at a neighbor's house—if you speak Cantonese you can join in whatever conversation is going on.
spots.price: MOP35 for a combo (rice, soup, and several dishes). If it's not enough to fill you up, there's no charge for another…

spots.name: Clube Militar
spots.desc: Built as a club for Portuguese military officers, it is now a classy restaurant.

spots.name: A Lorcha
spots.desc: Many say this is one of the best restaurants in Macau. Book in advance if you come on a weekend or Hong Kong holiday. Famous for their clams, African chicken and charcoal grilled items.

spots.name: Porto Exterior
spots.desc: Bustling, unpretentious restaurant with reasonably authentic and tasty Portuguese and Macanese fare. Try the arroz de cabidela (MOP 78) and wash it down with a glass of the house wine (MOP 35).

spots.name: Cafe Toscana
spots.desc: Great little pizzas, pasta and decent red wine. Just perfect when you are ready for a change from Chinese and Portuguese. Nearby are two great gelato places, Lemoncello and ?? - a nice way to finish your meal.

spots.name: Robuchon au Dôme
spots.desc: This French restaurant at the Grand Lisboa is operated by the famed Joël Robuchon. It is the only three Michelin star rated restaurant in Macau for the 2012 guide.
spots.price: Dinner can be expensive, with the top degustation menu costing MOP2,388 per person, but lunch is considered good value…

spots.name: 888 Gourmet Place
spots.desc: a food court on the second floor offering a variety of meals and buffets with variations of Japanese, Thai, Chinese and Sushi options. It's one of Macau's popular dining outlets. With a casual setting, it's a great eatery with loads of variety for a delicious quick meal.

spots.name: Margaret's Café e Nata
spots.desc: Macau's second most famous pastel de nata (egg tart) spot - the owner used to be married to the famous Lord Stow of Coloane - has a much lower profile. In addition to platefuls of piping-hot egg tarts (10 patacas), they also have a good range of pastries and sandwiches made to order. Take a cup of espresso and sit on the terrace outside.

spots.name: Hard Rock Cafe
spots.addr: City of Dreams, Hard Rock Hotel, 2/F, Coloane-Taipa
